claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by incipient spinodal decomposition.
A composition-dependent free-energy instability triggers continuous nanoscale compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations lower the nucleation barrier for a secondary-phase transformation.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be placed in a high-temperature BCC state by annealing at approximately 1250°C.
Homogenization at 1250°C produces a uniform single-phase BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy.
Annealing the homogenized alloy at approximately 900°C for 1–20 hours promotes incipient spinodal decomposition.
Maintaining stress-free conditions isolates the intrinsic effect of composition-dependent thermodynamic instability.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations are a structural indicator of incipient spinodal decomposition.
The specific Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 composition creates negative curvature in the free-energy surface.
Negative free-energy curvature causes spontaneous, continuous compositional modulation.
Short annealing at 900°C will produce measurable nanoscale compositional modulations before a distinct new phase appears.
With prolonged annealing, the compositional fluctuations will coarsen into a developed secondary phase.
The transformation kinetics will have a curve characteristic of spinodal decomposition.
Samples rapidly quenched from 1250°C will retain a stress-free, compositionally homogeneous BCC state with minimal compositional modulation.
Rapidly quenched controls will exhibit delayed or absent phase transformation compared with samples annealed at 900°C.
At approximately 900°C, atomic mobility is sufficient for compositional redistribution while still allowing spinodal fluctuations to develop.
At significantly higher temperatures, rapid diffusion may obscure the proposed spinodal mechanism.
At sufficiently low temperatures, atomic mobility may be inadequate for the proposed decomposition.
Ordering behavior in Al-containing Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys depends on Al content and temperature.
Observation of distinct nucleation-and-growth behavior rather than continuous time-dependent fluctuations would falsify the proposed spinodal mechanism.
